Construction of the Credit and Bank Channel of Macro-Finance Regime Switching Model

宏观金融机制转换模型中信贷与银行渠道模块的构建

✍ Dong Liu 📅 October 2026 💬 Comments welcome
Draft status. All results below come from the real-data run of the Appendix code, on data retrieved on 15–16 October 2026. The estimation sample is 1986Q2–2024Q1 (152 quarters). Comments are welcome before the note is finalised.

Abstract

This note documents the construction and verification of the credit and bank channel, the second of three modules in a regime-switching macro-finance model. It is estimated conditional on the New Keynesian DSGE core of Module 1, in the staged sequence implied by the system's lower-triangular transition matrix. Part One covers data acquisition (a Baa–Treasury credit spread, the Gilchrist–Zakrajšek excess bond premium, a Ken French bank-industry portfolio, the He–Kelly–Manela intermediary capital ratio, and the Gomme–Ravikumar–Rupert return on business capital), a bank-equity regime proxy calibrated against a fixed list of financial accidents, and an informative prior built from the excess bond premium. Part Two develops the block in full: a semi-structural closure of the Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist financial accelerator that treats intermediary leverage as an observed state, a Kalman filter verified first on simulated data with known parameters, full-likelihood Bayesian estimation by adaptive Metropolis, a Kim (1994) filter that estimates the transition matrix inside the likelihood, and a test of whether the credit-stress regime and Module 1's monetary-policy regime are one Markov chain or two.

Three design problems are found and fixed along the way, and each is reported. First, the framework's net-worth equation carries a unit root; the BGG survival rate removes it. Second, the framework's proxy for the return on capital is built from the same credit spread the block is meant to explain, which turns the arbitrage condition into an identity; it is replaced by an independent national-accounts return. Third, a first version of the regime synchronisation test, using per-lag HAC p-values, wrongly called independent chains "coupled" 51.5% of the time in simulation; a Markov-surrogate version brings that false-positive rate to 7.0% with no loss of power against true coupling.

The headline finding is that the leverage-to-spread link is much weaker than the textbook accelerator. The posterior mean of the leverage elasticity is $\psi\approx0.013$ (89% interval 0.010–0.017), about one-fifteenth of the BGG-implied prior mean of 0.20, and it barely moves under an alternative inflation measure. The arbitrage restriction is centred on its BGG value ($\lambda\approx1.05$), but its interval (0.27–1.81) is too wide to be a test. The block finds two credit-stress episodes, 2008–09 and the 2020 pandemic, with an expected duration of about three quarters. In those episodes the leverage elasticity is roughly four times larger than in normal times, as intermediary-asset-pricing theory predicts, but that contrast disappears when the GZ spread replaces the Baa spread. The credit-stress regime lines up closely with NBER recessions, while Module 1's monetary-policy regime is statistically independent of both. The regime layer of the unified model should therefore carry two chains rather than one. A regression of Module 1's IS shocks on lagged credit shocks finds no significant feedback, so the staged structure is not contradicted by the data.

Keywords: financial accelerator, intermediary leverage, external finance premium, excess bond premium, Kalman filter, adaptive Metropolis, Markov-switching, Kim filter, regime synchronisation

Part One · Data & Priors

1.1 Model Setup

The credit and bank channel is the second of three modules in the regime-switching macro-finance model laid out in the framework article. Because the system's transition matrix is lower-triangular, this module is estimated conditional on Module 1: the output gap $\hat x_t$, inflation $\pi_t$ and the policy rate $i_t$ enter here as given, and nothing estimated here feeds back into Module 1. The framework writes the block as three log-linearised Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist (BGG, 1999) equations: an external finance premium that rises with leverage, a net-worth accumulation equation, and an arbitrage condition linking the premium to the expected excess return on capital.

Those equations cannot be embedded in Module 1 as written. BGG's leverage term $\hat q_t+\hat k_{t+1}-\hat n_{t+1}$ needs a price of capital $q_t$ and a capital stock $k_t$, and Module 1's three-equation core has neither: it contains no investment decision and no capital accumulation. Two routes are available. One is to add a capital block to Module 1, which would change a module that is already estimated. The other, adopted here, is a semi-structural closure: leverage is treated as a state variable that is observed (with error) in the data, intermediary assets follow a reduced-form law of motion driven by Module 1's states, and the three BGG relations are kept as the structural content of the block.

A second reinterpretation follows from the data. In BGG the leveraged agent is an entrepreneur; the observables available for the U.S. (bank equity, dealer balance sheets) describe financial intermediaries. The block is therefore read in the Gertler–Kiyotaki (2010) and Gertler–Karadi (2011) sense, in which intermediaries hold claims on business capital, earn its return $R^k_t$, and face a premium that rises with their own leverage. Writing $n_t$ for intermediary net worth and $a_t$ for intermediary assets (both 100 × log deviations from trend), leverage is $\ell_t\equiv a_t-n_t$, the counterpart of BGG's $\hat q_t+\hat k_{t+1}-\hat n_{t+1}$. The block is:

External Finance Premium (regime-dependent)

$$ \hat s_t = \psi(S^c_t)\,\ell_t + e^s_t, \qquad e^s_t=\rho_s e^s_{t-1}+u^s_t,\quad u^s_t\sim N\!\big(0,\sigma_s^2(S^c_t)\big) $$

Net-Worth Accumulation (with BGG survival rate $\theta$)

$$ n_t = \theta\, n_{t-1} + \frac{\theta\bar\ell}{4}\big(R^k_t - r_{t-1}\big) + \frac{\theta}{4}\, r_{t-1} + \varepsilon^n_t,\qquad \varepsilon^n_t\sim N\!\big(0,\sigma_n^2(S^c_t)\big) $$

Asset Demand (semi-structural closure, carries $\Gamma_{21}$)

$$ a_t = \rho_a\, a_{t-1} + \gamma_x \hat x_t - \gamma_r\, r_t + \varepsilon^a_t,\qquad \varepsilon^a_t\sim N(0,\sigma_a^2) $$

Arbitrage Restriction

$$ E_t\big[R^k_{t+1}-r_t\big] = \lambda\,\hat s_t, \qquad \text{BGG: } \lambda = 1 $$

Here $r_t = i_t-\pi_t$ is the ex-post real policy rate built from Module 1's observables, $R^k_t$ is the realised real return on business capital, $S^c_t\in\{0,1\}$ is a latent credit regime (0 = normal, 1 = stress), and every variable is a deviation from its sample mean. Rates and spreads are in annualised percentage points, and the factor $1/4$ converts them to the quarterly returns that accumulate into net worth. Three choices in this specification depart from the framework article, and each is argued for in Part Two rather than here:

  • the survival rate $\theta<1$ in the net-worth equation, which the framework's version omits (Section 2.1.2);
  • an independent proxy for $R^k_t$ in place of the framework's "corporate spread plus Treasury yield" construction (Section 2.2.3);
  • $\lambda$ is estimated rather than imposed, so that the BGG arbitrage condition becomes a testable restriction instead of an assumption (Section 2.3).

The asset-demand equation is where Module 1 enters. Its loadings $\gamma_x$ and $\gamma_r$, together with the appearance of $r_t$ and $R^k_t-r_{t-1}$ in the net-worth equation, are the concrete form of the cross-block matrix $\Gamma_{21}$ in the framework's transition equation. Leverage then moves for two reasons: asset demand responds to the macro state, and net worth absorbs capital-return surprises. This second channel is the core BGG mechanism, and the block keeps it: a fall in net worth with sticky assets raises $\ell_t$ and therefore $\hat s_t$.

Three coverage problems shaped these choices, in the same way the withdrawal of ISM data from FRED shaped Module 1's regime proxy.

  • Bank equity before 1999. The framework names XLF as the bank-equity proxy, but XLF begins trading only in December 1998, leaving 14 years of the 1985–2026 sample uncovered. The Ken French "Banks" portfolio covers the full sample and is built on a consistent industry definition.
  • Option-adjusted spreads. The ICE BofA indices named in the framework begin only in the late 1990s. The monthly Baa–10y spread covers 1985 onward and is used as the baseline. The GZ spread, built from firm-level bond prices, is the more refined measure and is used in Variant A.
  • The binding series. The sample ends where the shortest series ends. The GRR return-to-capital series runs to 2024Q1, and that is where the estimation sample ends. It starts in 1986Q2 because Module 1's year-over-year inflation begins in 1986Q1 and the real rate enters with one lag, giving 152 quarters in all. One data-quality note: the June 2025 HKM file lists 2025Q1 twice with different values (0.0845 and 0.0745). That quarter falls outside the sample, and A.1 keeps the first entry.

Two mapping caveats deserve stating at the outset. The HKM ratio measures the market-value capital ratio of primary dealers' holding companies, a narrower set of institutions than the Banks portfolio. And GRR's return includes capital gains on the capital stock, so it is noisier than a pure income yield; the same file carries a version without capital gains (return_business_capital_after_tax_no_gain), which is the natural alternative if the arbitrage restriction turns out to be swamped by noise. Both caveats are discussed again in Section 3.3.

1.3 Constructing the Regime Proxy

The framework's trigger is $R^{bank}_t-R^{mkt}_t<-1.5\sigma$. Read literally on quarterly returns, it would flag single bad quarters, while the regularity it is meant to capture is sustained underperformance. The proxy is therefore built on a two-quarter window:

$$ D_t=\sum_{j=0}^{1}\big(r^{bank}_{t-j}-r^{mkt}_{t-j}\big),\qquad z_t=\frac{D_t-\bar D}{\mathrm{sd}(D)},\qquad S^{c,\text{proxy}}_t = \mathbf 1\{z_t<-k\} $$

using log returns from the Ken French portfolios. The framework calls the threshold $k$ a choice of quantile rather than a structural parameter, and says it should be calibrated to the historical frequency of financial accidents. To keep the calibration from being tuned after the fact, the list of accident quarters was fixed before the proxy was computed: 1990Q4 (the commercial real-estate bank crunch), 1998Q3 (Russia/LTCM), 2007Q4 and 2008Q3–2009Q1 (the global financial crisis), 2011Q3 (euro-area sovereign stress), 2020Q1 (the pandemic shock) and 2023Q1 (regional bank failures). For $k\in\{1.0,1.5,2.0\}$, A.1 reports how many events fall within one quarter of a trigger, the total number of trigger quarters, and the number of trigger quarters that match no event.

Threshold $k$Events hit (±1q)Trigger quartersUnmatched trigger quarters
1.09 / 9229
1.5 (framework)7 / 9113
2.05 / 962

Lowering the threshold to 1.0$\sigma$ catches every event but adds nine unmatched quarters, among them the 2016Q1–Q2 bank selloff and 1994Q4. Raising it to 2.0$\sigma$ cuts false alarms to two but misses four of the nine events. The framework's 1.5$\sigma$ is a reasonable middle: it misses 1998Q3 (LTCM) and 2011Q3 (euro-area stress), in which banks underperformed the market by about 10% within a single quarter but the two-quarter z-score reached only −1.1 and −1.4. Its three unmatched quarters are 1990Q1 and 1999Q4–2000Q1. The 1.5$\sigma$ proxy is kept as the baseline.

As with Module 1's CFNAI indicator, this proxy is an exogenous benchmark. Section 2.4 infers the credit regime endogenously from the block's own likelihood and compares the two.

1.4 The Excess Bond Premium as a Prior Source

Module 1 built its informative prior for the monetary-shock variance from high-frequency policy surprises, choosing Jarocinski–Karadi (2020) because it separates pure policy shocks from central-bank information shocks. The excess bond premium of Gilchrist and Zakrajšek (2012) plays the same role here. GZ decompose the firm-level credit spread into the part explained by expected default risk and a residual, the EBP, which they interpret as the risk-bearing capacity of the financial sector. That residual is the closest available empirical counterpart to the spread shock $e^s_t$: movement in the premium that is not explained by borrower fundamentals.

Because the block models $e^s_t$ as AR(1), the relevant prior object is the innovation variance, not the level variance. A.1 fits an AR(1) to quarterly-averaged EBP over 1985–2026 and takes the residual variance as the prior centre for $\sigma_s^2$. The estimates are $\hat\rho_{EBP}=0.834$ and $s^2=0.0935$ (annualised percentage points squared).

A Stated Overlap

Module 1's prior came from a source that was cleanly separate from its observables: policy surprises measured in 30-minute windows say nothing directly about the level of the fed funds rate. That separation does not hold here. The EBP is constructed from the same corporate bond market as the Baa spread, so the prior and the likelihood are not fully independent sources of information. In Variant A, where the GZ spread itself is the observable, the overlap is larger still. Two mitigations are used: the prior governs only the innovation variance, not the spread level, and Section 2.3 reports how much the posterior moves as the prior strength $\nu$ changes.

1.5 Informative Prior Construction

Shock and measurement-error variances use the scaled inverse-$\chi^2$ form from Module 1, $\sigma^2\sim\text{Inv-Gamma}(\nu/2,\ \nu s^2/2)$, with $\nu$ read as a number of virtual observations. The structural parameters need more care, because the framework lists two of them, the leverage elasticity $\psi$ and the steady-state leverage ratio $\bar\ell=\bar R^k\bar K/\bar N$, as calibrated. Module 1's central lesson was that a parameter conventionally calibrated (there, $\sigma=1$) can sit far from where the likelihood puts it (there, $\sigma\approx7.4$). The same logic is applied here. $\psi$ and $\bar\ell$ are estimated, with priors centred on their textbook calibrations, so that how far the posterior moves away is itself a result.

Translating BGG's Elasticity into This Block's Units

In BGG the quarterly gross premium has elasticity $\nu_{BGG}=0.05$ with respect to leverage, in log-decimal units. Here $\hat s_t$ is in annualised percentage points and $\ell_t$ is 100 × log, so a 1% rise in leverage maps to $4\times0.05=0.20$ annualised points:

$$ \psi_{\text{prior mean}} = 4\,\nu_{BGG} = 0.20 $$

The prior is wide (Gamma, s.d. 0.14). HKM leverage moves by tens of log points in a crisis, so a $\psi$ anywhere near 0.20 would imply spreads that move far more than they have historically. The calibration is a point of reference, not something the data are expected to confirm.

1.6 Summary of Part One

Part One produces an aligned quarterly panel of spreads, leverage, bank returns and capital returns, merged with Module 1's macro series; an exogenous credit-regime proxy calibrated against a fixed event list; and a prior set in which the two parameters the framework would have calibrated are instead estimated against their textbook values. Part Two starts from the interface with Module 1.

Part Two · Modeling & Estimation

2.1 Conditioning on Module 1 and the Stationarity Check

2.1.1 What Module 1 Hands Over

Staged estimation requires a decision on the form in which Module 1's output enters. There are three options: Module 1's observables directly, its Kalman-smoothed states, or draws from its posterior propagated through this module so that first-stage uncertainty is carried forward (the generated-regressor problem of Murphy and Topel, 1985). For the macro inputs, the first two options coincide in practice. In Module 1, $\hat x_t$, $\pi_t$ and $i_t$ are observed with measurement-error variance fixed at 1% of each series' sample variance, so the smoothed states and the data differ by a negligible margin, and the posterior uncertainty that would enter through the third option is negligible too. Module 2 therefore uses the observables directly. The same argument does not apply to Module 1's filtered regime probabilities, which are model-generated objects with substantial uncertainty; Section 2.5 returns to that.

2.1.2 A Unit Root in the Framework's Net-Worth Equation

The framework writes net-worth accumulation as

$$ \hat n_{t+1} = \frac{\bar R^k\bar K}{\bar N}\big(\hat R^k_t-\hat R_{t-1}\big)+\hat R_{t-1}+\hat n_t $$

with a unit coefficient on $\hat n_t$. That makes net worth a random walk with drift terms: any shock to it is permanent, and the block's transition matrix has an eigenvalue of exactly one. A stationary Kalman filter cannot be initialised from its unconditional distribution under that structure, and the model would have no reason for bank equity to recover after an accident. BGG themselves avoid this by having only a fraction $\theta$ of entrepreneurs survive each period, the rest consuming their equity on exit. Restoring that term gives the equation in Section 1.1, with $\theta=0.9728$ as in BGG. A.2 checks the eigenvalues of the transition matrix under both versions:

Net-worth equationEigenvalue moduli of $T$Verdict
Framework form ($\theta=1$)1.0000, 0.8000, 0.7000, 0.0000Unit root
BGG survival ($\theta=0.9728$)0.9728, 0.8000, 0.7000, 0.0000Stable

The remaining eigenvalues are $\rho_a$ and $\rho_s$ at their prior means and the zero root of the lag-identity row. The half-life of a net-worth shock is $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.9728 = 25.1$ quarters. That is slow, and Section 3.1 notes the consequence: because $\theta$ is calibrated, this persistence is imposed rather than estimated, so the block cannot by itself test the regularity that "banks keep underperforming for longer."

2.1.3 $\Gamma_{21}$ Diagnostics

Before the structural estimation, A.2 runs two reduced-form regressions (Newey–West, 4 lags) that show how much the macro state moves the credit block: the realised excess return on capital $R^k_t-r_{t-1}$ on $(\hat x_t,r_t)$, and the change in HKM leverage on $(\hat x_t,r_t)$. It also regresses next-quarter excess returns on the current spread, which gives a model-free first look at $\lambda$.

Regressionon $\hat x_t$on $r_t$R²
$R^k_t-r_{t-1}$0.176 (t = 0.67)−1.405 (t = −12.18)0.569
$\Delta\ell^{HKM}_t$1.027 (t = 1.79)−0.601 (t = −1.69)0.021
$R^k_{t+1}-r_t$ on spread$_t$slope 0.919 (s.e. 0.936)

The large coefficient on $r_t$ in the first row is mostly mechanical, not economic. The excess return subtracts $r_{t-1}$ by construction, and the real rate is so persistent that $r_t$ stands in for $r_{t-1}$. The informative rows are the other two. Dealer leverage rises with the output gap and falls with the real rate, but these two variables explain only 2% of its quarterly changes, so most leverage movement originates inside the financial sector. The reduced-form slope of next-quarter capital returns on the spread is close to 1, the BGG value, but with a standard error just as large. That foreshadows the weak identification of $\lambda$ found in Section 2.3.

2.2 The Kalman Filter: Verification on Simulated and Real Data

2.2.1 Stochastic Singularity

Module 1 reached its specification with three structural shocks after a first version with one shock was stochastically singular. Here the count is set up front. The block has four observables (the spread, HKM leverage, the bank excess return, and next quarter's excess return on capital), three structural shocks ($\varepsilon^n,\varepsilon^a,u^s$) and four measurement errors, one per observable. The measurement-error variances are estimated (Table 2), so the innovation covariance $F_t$ is full rank by construction. The measurement matrix $Z$ itself has rank 3, not 4, because the arbitrage row is $\lambda$ times the spread row. That does not leave a state unidentified: identification requires observability of the pair $(T,Z)$, and A.3 checks that the observability matrix $[Z;\,ZT;\,ZT^2;\,ZT^3]$ has full rank 4. Net worth is pinned down through the bank-return row, $n_t-n_{t-1}$, together with the dynamics.

2.2.2 State-Space Representation

State (Transition) Equation

$$ \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} n_t\\ n_{t-1}\\ a_t\\ e^s_t\end{pmatrix}}_{\alpha_t} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\theta&0&0&0\\1&0&0&0\\0&0&\rho_a&0\\0&0&0&\rho_s\end{pmatrix}}_{T}\alpha_{t-1} + \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\theta\bar\ell/4&\theta/4\\0&0&0&0\\ \gamma_x&-\gamma_r&0&0\\0&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}}_{B\ (\Gamma_{21})}\begin{pmatrix}\hat x_t\\ r_t\\ R^k_t-r_{t-1}\\ r_{t-1}\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon^n_t\\0\\ \varepsilon^a_t\\ u^s_t\end{pmatrix} $$

Observation (Measurement) Equation

$$ \begin{pmatrix}\text{spread}_t\\ \text{lev}^{HKM}_t\\ r^{bank}_t-r^f_t\\ R^k_{t+1}-r_t\end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}-\psi&0&\psi&1\\-1&0&1&0\\1&-1&0&0\\-\lambda\psi&0&\lambda\psi&\lambda\end{pmatrix}}_{Z(S^c_t)}\alpha_t + \begin{pmatrix}m^s_t\\m^\ell_t\\m^b_t\\m^e_t\end{pmatrix} $$

Two features need comment. First, there is no rational-expectations solve. The only forward-looking relation, the arbitrage restriction, enters as a measurement equation for the realised next-quarter excess return, with the forecast error absorbed in $m^e_t$. Section 2.1 of Module 1 needed an undetermined-coefficients solver and a multi-start determinacy scan; nothing of that kind is needed here, and the corresponding check is the eigenvalue condition of Section 2.1.2. Second, the realised excess return appears twice: as an input $R^k_t-r_{t-1}$ to the net-worth equation at $t$, and as an observable $R^k_{t+1}-r_t$ at $t$. This is a valid prediction-error decomposition, because the filter conditions on $y_{1:t-1}$, which already contains $R^k_t-r_{t-1}$, before the period-$t$ update.

2.2.3 The $R^k$ Proxy and an Identification Trap

An Identification Trap Worth Reporting

The framework notes that $\hat R^k_t$ has no direct free series and approximates it by combining a corporate-bond spread with the Treasury yield of matching maturity. That construction makes $R^k_{t}-R_{t}$ equal to the corporate spread by definition. Substituted into the arbitrage condition $E_t[\hat R^k_{t+1}-\hat R_t]=\hat s_t$, with $\hat s_t$ measured by the same spread, the equation becomes an identity. The likelihood then contains no information about $\lambda$, and the net-worth equation would be driven by the very spread the block is meant to explain. The problem is not visible in estimation output; a sampler would simply return the prior for $\lambda$.

The replacement is the Gomme–Ravikumar–Rupert (2011) real after-tax return on business capital, built from national-accounts income flows and capital-stock revaluations. It never touches a bond yield, so the arbitrage restriction becomes a genuine cross-equation restriction: it states that the bond-market premium should forecast the realised national-accounts return on capital one-for-one. The cost of this proxy is noise, since realised returns include capital gains, and that is why its forecast-error variance has a weak prior centred on half of its sample variance.

2.2.4 Verification on Simulated Data

Before any real data are used, the full estimation pipeline is run on data simulated from the block at known parameter values, with sample length $N=157$, close to the 152-quarter real sample. This is the analogue of Module 1's impulse-response check on its RE solver: it verifies that the code recovers what it is supposed to recover, separately from whether the model fits the data. A.8 runs three tests.

(1) Single-regime MCMC recovery. Data are simulated from a single regime; the $\sigma_s^2$ prior is deliberately centred 50% above the true value, to mimic an imperfect EBP prior; and the sampler of Section 2.3 is run on four chains.

Table 3. Single-regime parameter recovery on simulated data (A.8, test 1): four chains, second half of each retained. The true value lies inside the 89% interval for 11 of 14 parameters.

The sampler mixes well: acceptance rates are 0.23–0.26 across the four chains, every parameter has ESS above 550, and split-$\hat R$ is at most 1.013. Four parameters ($\rho_a$, $\gamma_x$, $\sigma_n^2$, $\sigma^2_{m^s}$) sit at 1.011–1.013, just above the 1.01 criterion, with the 16,000-iteration chains used here; the real-data run uses 30,000. With 89% intervals, one or two misses out of 14 would be expected by chance, and three occur. They share one cause. The prior for the leverage measurement-error variance, centred by the 5%-of-variance rule at 52.1, is thirteen times the true value of 4.0, and the posterior settles at 11.3. Leverage noise that is attributed to measurement error then has to be offset elsewhere: the net-worth shock variance is overstated (74.8 against 60), and $\psi$ is pushed slightly up (0.023 against 0.020, interval [0.0205, 0.0259]). The bias in $\psi$ is small in economic terms, but it is a bias, and Section 3.3 lists the measurement-error prior as technical debt.

The most important result for the real-data run concerns $\lambda$. Its interval, [0.07, 0.87], covers the true 0.80, but it is the widest relative to its value of any structural parameter, and the posterior mean of 0.47 is well below the truth. Realised returns on capital are noisy, so one quarter of spread information says little about them, and the arbitrage restriction is only weakly identified in a sample of this length. On real data, an interval that includes 1 should therefore be read as an absence of evidence against BGG, not as confirmation; only an interval that clearly excludes 1 is informative.

(2) Kim-filter recovery. A two-regime path is simulated from $p_{00}=0.95$, $p_{11}=0.80$ (58 stress quarters out of 157), with $\psi$, $\sigma_n^2$ and $\sigma_s^2$ switching. The Kim quasi-MLE of Section 2.4 is run with the non-switching parameters fixed at their true values, which mirrors the real application, where they are fixed at posterior means.

2.2.5 Fixed-Parameter Verification on Real Data

A.3 runs the filter and the Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother on the real data at prior-mean parameters and checks the conditions that must hold before estimation: the observability rank condition, $F_t$ positive definite in every period, and a finite log-likelihood. One-step-ahead RMSE relative to each observable's standard deviation is reported as a baseline for the estimated parameters to improve on, not as a pass/fail test. At prior means it is not expected to be below 1 for the spread: with $\psi$ at 0.20, the prior-mean block overstates how much spreads respond to leverage, and in the synthetic smoke test the spread RMSE ratio at prior means was 1.37.

All three conditions pass. The observability matrix has rank 4, the smallest eigenvalue of $F_t$ over the sample is 2.40, and the log-likelihood at prior means is −2545.8. The RMSE/s.d. ratios are 2.00 for the spread, 0.76 for leverage, 1.08 for the bank return and 1.14 for next-quarter capital returns. The spread ratio of 2.00 is the expected symptom of $\psi=0.20$: at that value the block predicts spread movements twice as large as the data contain, an early sign of the result in Section 2.3.

2.3 Full-Likelihood Bayesian Estimation

2.3.1 Likelihood and Posterior Kernel

For a parameter vector $\vartheta$ of 14 elements, the log-likelihood is the Kalman prediction-error decomposition

$$ \log L(\vartheta)=-\tfrac12\sum_{t=1}^{N}\Big[k_t\log 2\pi+\log|F_t(\vartheta)|+v_t(\vartheta)'F_t(\vartheta)^{-1}v_t(\vartheta)\Big] $$

where $k_t$ is the number of observables available at $t$ (the last quarter has no $R^k_{t+1}$). The filter is initialised at the unconditional state distribution, which exists because of Section 2.1.2. The posterior kernel adds the log-priors of Table 2, and sampling takes place in an unconstrained space (logs for positive parameters, logits for persistence parameters) with the matching Jacobian terms.

2.3.2 Sampler Choice

Module 1 used PyMC's black-box Metropolis step and found that $\kappa$ never reached $\hat R<1.03$, most plausibly because a one-parameter-at-a-time proposal mixes poorly along its posterior correlation with $\phi_\pi$. This module avoids that failure by design. The sampler is the adaptive Metropolis algorithm of Haario, Saksman and Tamminen (2001):

  1. locate the posterior mode by L-BFGS from several starts;
  2. initialise the joint Gaussian proposal at the inverse numerical Hessian at the mode, scaled by $2.38^2/d$;
  3. adapt the proposal covariance to the running sample covariance during the first half of each chain only;
  4. freeze the proposal for the second half, which is the half retained, so the retained draws come from a valid fixed-kernel Markov chain.

Correlated parameters are therefore proposed jointly. Four chains of 30,000 iterations are run (about ten milliseconds per likelihood evaluation, so a few minutes per chain); split-$\hat R$ and the effective sample size are reported for every parameter.

Convergence Criterion

A parameter is reported as converged when split-$\hat R<1.01$ and ESS > 400 across chains. Anything that fails is reported as such, as Module 1 did for $\kappa$. In the baseline run every parameter passes: the largest $\hat R$ is 1.006, the smallest ESS is 1,105, and acceptance rates are 0.235–0.255 across the four chains. Module 1's $\kappa$ problem does not recur.

Three numbers carry the section, and each is matched to a pre-stated reading:

  • $\psi$ relative to 0.20 measures how far the market leverage of intermediaries is from BGG's calibrated accelerator.
  • $P(\lambda<1\mid Y)$ and the 89% interval for $\lambda$ test the arbitrage restriction. An interval excluding 1 means bond spreads do not forecast the national-accounts return on capital one-for-one.
  • The sign of $\gamma_x$ shows whether intermediary balance sheets expand with the output gap (procyclical leverage in the Adrian–Shin, 2010, sense) or contract with it.

Each reading can now be filled in. $\psi$ is 0.013, one-fifteenth of the BGG-implied 0.20, with an interval that excludes the calibration by a wide margin. A 10-log-point rise in dealer leverage, about a third of its sample standard deviation, widens the Baa spread by 13 basis points. $\lambda$ has posterior mean 1.05, and $P(\lambda<1\mid Y)=0.46$. The posterior is centred almost exactly on the BGG restriction, but its 89% interval [0.27, 1.81] is about as wide as the synthetic test predicted (Section 2.2.4), so the data neither confirm nor reject the arbitrage condition. $\gamma_x$ is positive (0.42), so intermediary assets expand with the output gap, but its interval includes zero. The steady-state leverage ratio $\bar\ell$ comes in at 1.09, well below its prior mean of 4 and below BGG's 2: bank equity responds to surprises in the national-accounts return on capital roughly one-for-one, not with the four-to-one amplification the calibration implies. Finally, the leverage measurement-error variance settles at 11.8, against a prior centre of 77.7, so the data pull it well away from the prior that biased the synthetic test.

The EBP prior hardly matters. At the posterior mode, $\sigma_s^2$ is 0.0668, 0.0677 and 0.0698 for $\nu=3,6,15$ against a prior centre of 0.0935, and $\psi$ is 0.0135, 0.0135 and 0.0134. The likelihood dominates the prior across this range, as it did for Module 1's monetary-shock variance.

2.4 Regime-Switching: Endogenizing the Credit State

Three parameters switch with $S^c_t$: the leverage elasticity $\psi$, the net-worth shock variance $\sigma_n^2$, and the spread-shock variance $\sigma_s^2$. The other parameters are fixed at their Section 2.3 posterior means. The switching set follows He and Krishnamurthy (2013): when the intermediary's capital constraint binds, the premium becomes more sensitive to intermediary equity, and balance-sheet shocks are larger.

2.4.1 The Kim Filter with a Persistent State

The Kim (1994) filter runs, for each regime pair $(S^c_{t-1}=i,S^c_t=j)$, a Kalman step from the regime-$i$ collapsed state; it weights the four likelihoods by $p_{ij}$ and the prior regime probabilities, and then collapses the four posterior states back to two by moment matching. There is one implementation difference from Module 1 that matters. Module 1's state consisted of iid structural shocks, so restarting each step from a zero prior mean and covariance $Q$ discarded nothing. Here the state ($n_t$, $a_t$, $e^s_t$) is persistent, so the collapsed mean and covariance must be carried from period to period, which is the full Kim recursion.

2.4.2 Labelling and Estimation

Regimes are labelled by the net-worth shock variance, $\sigma_n^2(1)>\sigma_n^2(0)$, imposed through the parameterisation $\sigma_n^2(1)=\sigma_n^2(0)(1+e^z)$. This anchors "stress" to the definition used by the bank-equity proxy: large shocks to intermediary equity. The ordering of $\psi(1)$ and $\psi(0)$ is left free, so the He–Krishnamurthy prediction $\psi(1)>\psi(0)$ is a test rather than an assumption.

The transition matrix is estimated inside the Kim-filter likelihood, jointly with the six regime-dependent parameters, by quasi-maximum likelihood with delta-method standard errors from the numerical Hessian. This closes a gap noted in Module 1, where $(p_{00},p_{11})$ were taken from the empirical transition frequencies of the CFNAI proxy.

A Stated Limitation on Model Comparison

A likelihood-ratio test of two regimes against one does not have its usual $\chi^2$ distribution here. Under the null, the transition probabilities and the regime-1 parameters are not identified, which is the nuisance-parameter problem analysed by Hansen (1992). The regime-switching and single-regime log-likelihoods and the BIC are reported for information only; they are not a formal test.

The evaluation criterion is the one Module 1 set for its own regime path. High agreement between the filtered $P(S^c_t=1\mid Y_{1:t})$ and the exogenous bank-equity proxy would validate the proxy as an adequate simplification; material divergence would favour the endogenous path.

The filtered probability exceeds 0.5 in nine quarters, forming two episodes: 2008Q1–2009Q3 and 2020Q1–Q2. It agrees with the 1.5$\sigma$ proxy in 93.4% of quarters (correlation 0.491). The high agreement rate partly reflects that both indicators are zero most of the time, so the correlation is the more telling number. The divergences are informative. The proxy fires in 1990 and 1999Q4–2000Q1, quarters the endogenous regime does not flag. The second episode shows a weakness of any bank-minus-market proxy: banks lagged a technology-led market rally, which is relative underperformance, not intermediary distress. The endogenous regime, which sees leverage, spreads and bank returns together, is the better measure, and the proxy is retained only as the benchmark.

Three further results. First, $\psi(1)=0.027$ against $\psi(0)=0.007$: the leverage elasticity is about four times larger in the stress regime, as He and Krishnamurthy (2013) predict, and the two estimates are separated by more than three standard errors. Because the regimes were labelled by net-worth shock variance, this ordering is a result, not an assumption. Second, the expected durations are 46 quarters for the normal regime and 3.3 quarters for stress. Third, the regime-switching log-likelihood is −1516.3 against −1558.0 for the single-regime block, and the BIC falls from 3131.1 to 3072.8; with the caveat above, the data favour switching.

2.5 Regime Synchronisation with Module 1

The framework article left three questions open about its regime layer. This section answers the first of them for the two modules now estimated: do the credit-stress regime $S^c_t$ and Module 1's monetary-policy regime $S^m_t$ belong to one Markov chain, to two chains that are coupled with a lead or lag, or to two independent chains? The answer determines the structure of the unified model:

VerdictImplication for the regime layer of the unified model
Single chainOne $S_t$ with $K=2$ drives both blocks; the framework's original specification stands.
Coupled chainsA product chain with $K=4$ states and a restricted transition matrix in which one chain's past shifts the other's switching probabilities.
IndependentA product of two independent two-state chains; the blocks can keep separate regime filters.

2.5.1 Statistics and the Decision Rule

With $S^c_t$ and $S^m_t$ the binary paths obtained by thresholding each module's filtered probability at 0.5, A.6 computes:

  1. the Harding–Pagan (2002) concordance index $C=T^{-1}\sum_t[S^c_tS^m_t+(1-S^c_t)(1-S^m_t)]$, the share of quarters in which the two regimes agree;
  2. cross-correlations $\text{corr}(S^c_t,S^m_{t+k})$ for $|k|\le 8$, where $k>0$ means the credit regime leads;
  3. regime-Granger regressions: $S^c_t$ on $S^c_{t-1}$ and $S^m_{t-1}$, and the reverse;
  4. the $4\times4$ table of joint regime transitions.

The decision rule was fixed before any real-data result was seen:

Decision Rule (fixed ex ante)

Single chain if the contemporaneous correlation is significant at 5%, at least 0.5, concordance is at least 0.8, and the cross-correlation within $|k|\le4$ peaks at $k=0$. Coupled chains if some association within $|k|\le4$ is significant but the single-chain conditions fail. Independent otherwise.

2.5.2 A Failure Worth Reporting: the Size of the Test

A Failure Worth Reporting

The first implementation assessed significance with HAC (Newey–West, 4 lags) p-values, following Harding and Pagan (2006), applied separately at each of the nine lags $|k|\le4$. Run on simulated pairs of independent chains (persistence $p_{00}=0.95$, $p_{11}=0.80$, $N=157$), it classified them as "coupled" in 51.5% of 200 replications, against a nominal 5%. Two problems compound. Nine separate tests at 5% each give roughly a one-in-three chance of at least one false rejection even with exact p-values. And with regimes lasting 5 to 20 quarters, a four-lag HAC window understates the variance of the correlation estimate, so each individual test also over-rejects. Applied to real data, this rule would have reported coupling between Module 1 and Module 2 about half the time even if none existed.

The fix is a Markov-surrogate test, a parametric bootstrap under the null of independence. The transition matrix of $S^m_t$ is estimated from its own path, and 1,000 independent surrogate chains are simulated from it. These surrogates have the same persistence as $S^m_t$ but no relation to $S^c_t$. Significance at lag 0 uses the surrogate distribution of $|\text{corr}_0|$. The "any association" test uses the surrogate distribution of $\max_{|k|\le4}|\text{corr}_k|$, which handles the nine-lag search in a single statistic. The HAC version is still computed and printed, but no decision uses it. Table 4 gives the operating characteristics of both versions over 200 replications per design, with 5% classification noise added to the second chain:

It remains slightly above the nominal 5%, most likely because the surrogate transition matrix is estimated rather than known. The coupled design used here is strong (the second chain is an exact three-quarter lag of the first, apart from classification noise), so these power figures are an upper bound.

The credit regime and Module 1's monetary-policy regime are independent by the pre-set rule. Neither the contemporaneous correlation (0.07) nor the strongest correlation within four quarters is distinguishable from what two unrelated chains with the same persistence would produce. The regime-Granger regressions agree: neither regime's lag predicts the other at 5% (p = 0.21 and 0.08). The credit regime, by contrast, is synchronised with NBER recessions as tightly as the rule allows (concordance 0.954, correlation 0.69, peak at lag 0), and Module 1's regime is independent of recessions too. The same statistics were computed for each regime against NBER recessions as references, and they point to where the mismatch originates: in Module 1's regime definition, whose agreement with its own CFNAI proxy was only 65.4%. That regime is a Taylor-rule regime, identified by a weaker inflation response. It is high in 2021–2023, when policy responded slowly to inflation, a period with neither a recession nor credit stress, which is consistent with a reaction-function state rather than a business-cycle state.

One pattern sits below the significance threshold but is worth recording. The cross-correlogram of the filtered probabilities in Figure 7 is positive at $k=-2$ to $-8$ (about 0.25–0.29), so the monetary regime tends to precede credit stress by two to eight quarters, as in 2006–07. The HAC p-values on those bars are below 5%, but Section 2.5.2 showed that this kind of p-value rejects far too often. The surrogate test on the binary paths does not reject, and with only two credit-stress episodes it has little power. The lead is a hypothesis for the unified model, not a finding.

For the unified model the verdict means the framework's single regime chain is not supported. The regime layer should carry at least two chains: a credit/business-cycle chain, for which Module 2's regime is a good candidate, and a policy-reaction chain from Module 1. They can be modelled as independent, or as a product chain whose transition matrix allows the monetary state to shift credit-stress probabilities with a lag, if the lead above survives a longer sample.

One caveat applies whatever the verdict. Module 1's filtered probabilities enter here as data, but they are model-generated objects, and they inherit Module 1's myopic regime-switching approximation (its Section 3.2). Their uncertainty is not propagated into the test.

The framework's 1.5$\sigma$ gives the highest correlation, so the endogenous regime agrees with the framework's choice.

Part Three · Findings, Forecasting Implications & Limitations

3.1 What the Estimates Say About the Credit Channel

Four findings survived the robustness checks well enough to be stated plainly; a fifth did not and is stated with that qualification.

The leverage-to-spread link is weak. A leverage elasticity of 0.013 means that, in normal times, the market leverage of dealer intermediaries says little about the external finance premium. The 2007–08 episode puts a scale on this. From 2007Q2 to 2008Q4, HKM leverage rose by about 100 log points and the Baa spread widened by 3.9 percentage points. The single-regime block attributes 1.3 points of that widening to leverage (100 × 0.0133). Using the stress-regime elasticity of 0.027, the regime-switching block attributes 2.7 points, about two-thirds. Either way, a large part of the widening runs through the persistent spread shock $e^s_t$ (posterior persistence 0.90): movement in the premium that leverage does not explain, which is also how Gilchrist and Zakrajšek read the excess bond premium.

Credit stress is rare, short and synchronised with recessions. The block finds two stress episodes, 2008–09 and 2020, with an expected duration of about three quarters. The credit regime matches NBER recessions about as closely as two binary indicators can (concordance 0.95). The mild recessions of 1990–91 and 2001 do not register as credit stress, consistent with the reading that credit amplification is severe in some downturns and absent in others.

The monetary-policy regime and the credit regime are different objects. The framework assumed a single regime chain. The data reject that: Module 1's regime is a policy-reaction state, statistically unrelated to either credit stress or recessions. A hint that the policy state leads credit stress by two to eight quarters is recorded but not established.

The staged structure is not contradicted. Lagged credit shocks do not predict Module 1's IS shocks (joint p = 0.30), so the zero block above the diagonal of $T(S_t)$ is not rejected. With two stress episodes in the sample the test has limited power, so this is an absence of evidence against the staged structure, not a confirmation of it.

The stress-regime steepening of $\psi$ depends on the spread measure. With the Baa spread, the leverage elasticity is four times larger in stress, as intermediary-asset-pricing theory predicts. With the GZ spread, the contrast vanishes. The nonlinearity is plausible, but this module cannot establish it.

None of this says intermediary balance sheets are unimportant. It says how much of the premium a market-value leverage ratio can account for over 1986–2024, and that answer held up under two spread measures and two inflation measures.

The framework's financial-accident regularity, that the S&P 500 rebounds quickly while banks keep underperforming for longer, gets no structural support here. The persistence of net worth is governed by the calibrated $\theta$, so its 25-quarter half-life is built in rather than estimated. The closest estimated counterpart is the expected duration of the stress regime, and at about three quarters it is short.

What this means for forecasting

For credit spreads a quarter or two ahead, the estimates point to the spread's own persistence rather than to intermediary leverage. The spread shock has persistence 0.90, and leverage moves feed through at about 1 basis point per log point in normal times. A forecaster who tracks dealer leverage closely in calm periods is tracking a variable with little predictive weight for spreads.

The picture changes when the block switches into stress, and the switch is visible in real time: the filtered probability jumped above 0.75 in 2008Q1 and above 0.95 in 2020Q1, each time in the first quarter of the episode. Once in stress, at least with the Baa spread, the leverage elasticity roughly quadruples, so balance-sheet deterioration then becomes a meaningful driver of further widening. For stress-scenario design the implication is that spread shocks should be conditioned on the credit regime rather than scaled linearly from leverage. A scenario that calibrates the spread response to leverage from normal-time co-movement will understate the widening in a 2008-type episode. A scenario that uses stress-regime sensitivities throughout will overstate it in mild recessions like 1990–91 or 2001.

Finally, the short expected duration of stress (about three quarters) implies fast mean reversion once the episode ends. This should not be read as a statement about how long bank equity underperforms. Net-worth persistence is fixed by the calibrated $\theta$ (Section 3.3), so the block cannot speak to the "banks keep underperforming for longer" regularity.

Why the real economy might actually look like this

As in Module 1, nothing here identifies a mechanism. What follows are candidate readings from the broader literature, not something this module tested.

The small $\psi$ has several plausible sources. HKM leverage is a market-value ratio, so it rises mechanically whenever dealer equity prices fall, including for reasons that have nothing to do with lending capacity. Much of its variation is therefore noise with respect to the premium firms pay. The intermediaries whose balance sheets matter most for corporate borrowing costs may not be the primary dealers HKM measures: bond-market spreads are set by a broad investor base of insurers, mutual funds and pension funds. And the period after 2009 combined higher capital requirements and supervisory stress tests, which damp leverage swings, with central-bank backstops in 2008 and 2020 that cap how far spreads can widen for a given balance-sheet shock. Both work toward a flatter estimated relation.

The low $\bar\ell$ (about 1 rather than 4) most likely reflects the mapping rather than the economics. The GRR return covers all U.S. business capital and is built from national accounts, while bank equity prices respond to news about bank-specific assets and expected losses. One-for-one co-movement between the two is about what a loose link between those objects would produce.

The independence of the two regimes has a simpler explanation. Module 1's regime is identified from the Taylor rule, and policy regimes are set by central-bank behaviour that need not coincide with the business cycle: the 2021–23 episode, with policy slow to respond to inflation but no recession and no credit stress, is the clearest example. Credit stress, in contrast, is a property of the downturn itself.

We would stop short of calling any of this settled. Distinguishing these explanations needs measures of intermediary capital beyond primary dealers, and a longer sample with more stress episodes, neither of which this module had.

3.2 Staged Estimation Shuts Off the Accelerator

The defining claim of the financial-accelerator literature is feedback: falling net worth raises the premium, which cuts investment and output, which lowers net worth again. The lower-triangular structure that makes staged estimation possible removes the second half of that loop. Nothing in this module can move $\hat x_t$. What Module 2 estimates is therefore how the macro state drives the credit block, plus the propagation within the credit block (net worth to leverage to the premium). It does not estimate how much the credit block amplifies the business cycle. This should be kept in mind when reading $\psi$: a small $\psi$ means a weak link from leverage to spreads, not a weak accelerator in the general-equilibrium sense.

Whether this simplification is costly can be checked. If credit shocks feed back into output, they should predict the part of output that Module 1 cannot explain. A.7 regresses Module 1's filtered IS shock $\varepsilon^x_t$ on this module's smoothed spread innovation $u^s_{t-1}$ and net-worth shock $\varepsilon^n_{t-1}$ (Newey–West). A significant coefficient would mean the zero block above the diagonal of $T(S_t)$ is rejected by the data, and that the joint estimation the framework article left for future work is necessary rather than optional. The coefficient on $u^s_{t-1}$ is −3.70 (t = −1.29), the coefficient on $\varepsilon^n_{t-1}$ is −0.051 (t = −0.81), and the joint p-value is 0.295: no significant feedback. The point estimate on the spread shock has the sign the accelerator predicts, with a wider spread followed by a negative demand shock, but it is far from significant. One caveat: the IS shocks Module 1 saved come from its fixed-parameter filter (its Section 2.2, $\sigma=1$), not from the posterior of its Section 2.3.

3.3 Technical Debt in the Block and the Sampler

  • $\theta$ is calibrated. It governs net-worth persistence and was fixed at BGG's 0.9728 by the same reasoning that fixed Module 1's $\beta$. Section 3.1 shows that this choice is not innocuous for the bank-underperformance regularity.
  • An ex-post real rate. $r_t=i_t-\pi_t$ uses year-over-year realised inflation, not expected inflation. Module 1's model-implied $E_t\pi_{t+1}$ would be the consistent choice.
  • A mismatch of institutions. HKM leverage describes primary dealers' holding companies; the Banks portfolio covers a broader set of banks; GRR's return describes all business capital. The block treats them as three views of one intermediary sector.
  • Only part of the block switches. $\psi$, $\sigma_n^2$ and $\sigma_s^2$ switch; $\bar\ell$, $\lambda$ and the $\Gamma_{21}$ loadings do not. The regime parameters are estimated by quasi-MLE with the rest fixed at posterior means, not within one joint Bayesian posterior.
  • The leverage measurement-error prior. Centring each measurement-error prior at 5% of its observable's variance worked for every observable except leverage in the synthetic test, where the prior centre was thirteen times the true value and pulled the estimate up, along with two neighbouring parameters (Section 2.2.4). If the real-data posterior for $\sigma^2_{m^\ell}$ sits near its prior, a looser prior ($\nu=3$, or a centre of 1%) should be tried.
  • The surrogate test's size. Its false-positive rate is 7.0% rather than 5% (Section 2.5.2). Surrogating both chains, or adding a bootstrap of the estimated transition matrices, would likely bring it closer to nominal.

3.4 Unresolved Data and Verification Gaps

  • Sample end. The GRR return series ends in 2024Q1, so the last two years of Module 1's sample are not used. The 2023 regional bank stress is inside the window, but the endogenous regime does not flag it, and the 1.5$\sigma$ proxy flags only 2023Q2.
  • Only two stress episodes. Every regime-related result (the $\psi(1)$/$\psi(0)$ contrast, $p_{11}$, the synchronisation test) rests on 2008–09 and 2020. That is the main reason the GZ variant can overturn the regime contrast.
  • Data vintages. The EBP's entire history can be revised at each monthly update, and the HKM file is a June 2025 vintage. Results should record the download date.
  • Generated regressors in the synchronisation test. Module 1's regime probabilities enter as data (Section 2.5.3).
  • Limited power for $p_{11}$. In the synthetic test, $p_{11}$ was the least precisely recovered parameter (0.885 against 0.80) even with 58 stress quarters. The real sample has fewer distinct accidents.

3.5 Interface to Module 3

Module 3, the macro-finance affine term-structure model, takes this module's output in the same way this module took Module 1's. A.7 writes module2_states_for_module3.csv, containing the smoothed net worth $\hat n_t$, leverage $\ell_t$, the model-implied premium $\hat s_t$, the spread shock $e^s_t$, and the filtered credit-stress probability. In the framework's notation, these enter the term structure's price of risk $\lambda_t=\lambda_0+\lambda_1X_t$ through the block $\Gamma_{32}$. The synchronisation verdict of Section 2.5 also determines the form in which they arrive. If the regimes form a single chain, Module 3 conditions on one regime path. If they are coupled or independent, it must choose which chain, or which product state, its own term-premium regime responds to. That choice is the first design decision of the next note.
